NVDA.what: Sells accelerated-computing chips and the CUDA software around them to cloud providers, AI labs, enterprises and gamers.
NVDA.rev: Data centre is roughly 88-90% of revenue; gaming under 10%; auto and pro visualisation are rounding errors. By billing location, heavily Singapore/Taiwan/US, but end demand is US hyperscalers.
NVDA.gm: Gross margin around 70-75%. It is a fabless designer: TSMC makes the silicon, NVIDIA captures the architecture and software rent. CUDA lock-in lets it price to value, not cost.
NVDA.mgmt: Co-founder Jensen Huang has run it since 1993 and holds roughly 3-4% personally - unusually high for a company this size.
NVDA.comp: AMD (Instinct), Broadcom and Marvell (custom ASICs for hyperscalers), plus in-house silicon from Google TPU, Amazon Trainium, Microsoft Maia.
NVDA.moat: CUDA plus fifteen years of libraries, kernels and trained engineers. Switching cost is rewriting a code base, not swapping a chip. Add NVLink/networking scale and TSMC capacity priority.
NVDA.ind: Growing violently, but the growth is capex-funded by roughly five customers.
NVDA.risk: Hyperscalers succeeding with their own silicon for inference, so NVIDIA keeps training but loses the larger inference market - or an AI capex digestion year.
NVDA.implied: The multiple only works if data-centre revenue keeps compounding at a high double-digit rate for several more years with margins near 70%.
NVDA.debate: Bulls say compute demand is a decade-long build-out and NVIDIA is the toll booth. Bears say customer concentration plus custom silicon means peak share is behind it.
NVDA.disprove: Hyperscaler capex guidance cut; inventory and purchase commitments rising faster than revenue; gross margin drifting below 70%; a top customer publicly standardising on its own accelerator.

AAPL.what: Sells premium consumer hardware - iPhone above all - and an attached services bundle to about 2.4 billion active devices.
AAPL.rev: iPhone is roughly half of revenue; Services about a quarter but over 40% of gross profit; Mac, iPad and Wearables the rest. Americas ~42%, Europe ~26%, Greater China ~15%.
AAPL.gm: Blended gross margin around 47-48%: hardware near 37%, Services above 70%. Scale in procurement plus pricing power from the ecosystem.
AAPL.mgmt: John Ternus has taken over as CEO from Tim Cook, who led the company from 2011. Insider ownership is negligible (well under 1%) - this is a professionally managed, not founder-owned, company.
AAPL.comp: Samsung and Chinese OEMs (Huawei, Xiaomi) in phones; Google in services and search defaults; Microsoft in PCs.
AAPL.moat: Switching costs across iMessage, iCloud, App Store and Watch, plus a brand that supports a price premium and unmatched silicon-plus-software integration.
AAPL.ind: Smartphone units are flat globally; the growth is in price, services attach and installed base.
AAPL.risk: Losing the Google search default payment (roughly $20bn+ of near-pure profit) to an antitrust remedy, or a China demand and supply shock.
AAPL.implied: At a high-30s P/E the price implies services keeps compounding and a new hardware or AI cycle re-accelerates iPhone - not the low single-digit revenue growth of recent years.
AAPL.debate: Bulls point to the installed base as an annuity and buybacks shrinking the share count 2-3% a year. Bears say you are paying a growth multiple for a mature hardware business.
AAPL.disprove: Services growth slowing below ~10%; Greater China revenue declining two years running; an adverse final ruling on the Google default; gross margin rolling over.

GOOG.what: Sells advertising against search, YouTube and its network, plus cloud infrastructure, to advertisers and enterprises worldwide.
GOOG.rev: Search ~56%, YouTube ads ~10%, Network ~8%, Cloud ~14% and growing fastest, subscriptions/devices the rest. US ~48% of revenue.
GOOG.gm: Gross margin around 58%. Search has almost no marginal cost; Cloud and the traffic-acquisition payments to Apple and carriers drag the blend down.
GOOG.mgmt: Sundar Pichai is CEO; founders Page and Brin still control the company through Class B super-voting shares despite owning a minority of economics.
GOOG.comp: Meta and Amazon for ad dollars, Microsoft/OpenAI in search-like answers, AWS and Azure in cloud.
GOOG.moat: Default distribution, twenty-five years of query data, YouTube network effects and the cheapest compute per query via TPUs.
GOOG.ind: Digital advertising grows mid-to-high single digits; cloud and AI inference grow much faster.
GOOG.risk: Answer engines eating the ten blue links, so query volume monetises worse - plus antitrust remedies on default placements.
GOOG.implied: The multiple implies ad revenue keeps growing double digits while Cloud margin expands, with no structural erosion in search monetisation.
GOOG.debate: Bulls say Gemini plus TPUs plus distribution make it the best-positioned AI incumbent and Cloud is still underearning. Bears say search is the most disrupted profit pool on earth.
GOOG.disprove: Paid clicks growing while revenue per click falls for several quarters; Cloud growth decelerating below Azure; a forced unbundling of Chrome or Android defaults.

MSFT.what: Sells enterprise software, Azure cloud infrastructure and AI services to businesses, on subscription.
MSFT.rev: Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server) ~43%, Productivity (Office/M365, LinkedIn) ~32%, More Personal Computing (Windows, gaming, search) ~25%. US just over half.
MSFT.gm: Gross margin around 68-69%. Software is near-free to copy; the AI build-out of GPUs and data centres is pulling the cloud portion down toward the low 70s.
MSFT.mgmt: Satya Nadella has been CEO since 2014. Insider ownership is small; pay is heavily performance-share weighted.
MSFT.comp: Amazon AWS and Google Cloud in infrastructure; Google Workspace in productivity; Salesforce, ServiceNow and AWS in applications.
MSFT.moat: Enterprise switching costs across identity, Office and Windows, bundled licensing that makes each add-on nearly free, and a direct sales relationship with essentially every large company.
MSFT.ind: Enterprise IT spend is growing; the AI portion is growing much faster but is capital-hungry.
MSFT.risk: An AI capex cycle that does not convert into Azure revenue, leaving a huge depreciation charge against flat growth - or the OpenAI relationship souring.
MSFT.implied: A mid-30s P/E implies mid-teens revenue growth and stable margins despite capex now running above $80bn a year.
MSFT.debate: Bulls say Copilot and Azure AI are the largest enterprise attach opportunity ever. Bears say depreciation from the build-out will compress returns on capital for years.
MSFT.disprove: Azure growth slipping toward the mid-teens; capex rising while cloud gross margin falls; Copilot seat disclosures that never arrive; operating margin declining two years running.

AMZN.what: Sells retail goods and logistics to consumers and sells cloud computing and advertising to businesses.
AMZN.rev: Online stores ~40%, third-party seller services ~24%, AWS ~17% of revenue but the majority of operating profit, advertising ~9%, subscriptions ~7%. North America ~60%.
AMZN.gm: Reported gross margin is near 50% but mixes a low-margin retail business with AWS at roughly 60% operating margin and advertising at near-pure margin.
AMZN.mgmt: Andy Jassy is CEO; founder Jeff Bezos remains executive chairman and still owns roughly 8-9% - the largest insider stake among US mega caps.
AMZN.comp: Walmart and Temu/Shein in retail; Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud in infrastructure; Google and Meta in advertising.
AMZN.moat: Fulfilment network scale no one can replicate economically, Prime habit and lock-in, AWS switching costs and marketplace network effects.
AMZN.ind: E-commerce keeps taking share of retail; cloud and retail media both growing faster still.
AMZN.risk: AWS losing the AI workload race to Azure and Google while retail capex stays heavy - margin and multiple compress together.
AMZN.implied: The valuation implies AWS re-accelerates and retail operating margin keeps climbing toward high single digits.
AMZN.debate: Bulls say three high-margin businesses (AWS, ads, logistics-as-a-service) are hidden inside a retailer. Bears say capex of $100bn+ a year makes free cash flow unreliable.
AMZN.disprove: AWS growth trailing Azure and Google Cloud for several quarters; North America retail margin stalling; free cash flow negative in a non-recession year.

META.what: Sells targeted advertising against attention on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads to roughly 10 million advertisers.
META.rev: Advertising is about 98% of revenue; Reality Labs is a loss-making rounding error. US and Canada ~45% of revenue from ~10% of users.
META.gm: Gross margin around 81%. Once the data centre is built, another ad impression costs almost nothing; the cost is compute for ranking and recommendation.
META.mgmt: Mark Zuckerberg is founder-CEO and controls a majority of votes through Class B shares while owning about 13% of economics.
META.comp: Google/YouTube, TikTok and Amazon for advertising dollars and user time.
META.moat: Network effects across 3.4 billion daily users, an ad-ranking system improved by the largest behavioural data set outside Google, and advertiser switching costs.
META.ind: Digital ads grow mid-to-high single digits; Meta has been taking share via AI-driven ranking.
META.risk: Regulatory restriction on data use for targeting in the EU or US, or a spending pivot into AI and Reality Labs that never earns its cost of capital.
META.implied: The multiple implies high-teens ad growth continues while capex-driven depreciation is absorbed without margin loss.
META.debate: Bulls say AI recommendations keep lifting price per ad and Meta is the cheapest mega-cap on earnings. Bears point at $70bn+ annual capex and a founder who can spend it without asking.
META.disprove: Ad impressions growing while price per ad falls persistently; Reality Labs losses widening past $20bn; EU consent rulings that cut targeting reach; capex guidance rising with no revenue response.

AVGO.what: Sells networking and custom AI silicon to hyperscalers, plus infrastructure software (VMware, mainframe, security) to large enterprises.
AVGO.rev: Semiconductor solutions roughly 60% (AI networking and custom accelerators the growth engine), infrastructure software roughly 40% after VMware. Heavily concentrated in a handful of customers.
AVGO.gm: Gross margin around 65-78% depending on mix - software is high 80s, custom silicon lower. Broadcom buys mature franchises and raises prices rather than chasing volume.
AVGO.mgmt: Hock Tan has run it since 2006 and is one of the highest-paid, most disciplined capital allocators in semis; his stake is meaningful but modest.
AVGO.comp: NVIDIA and Marvell in AI silicon and networking; Cisco and Arista in switching; Nutanix and cloud providers against VMware.
AVGO.moat: Deep custom-ASIC co-design relationships with a few hyperscalers, essentially monopoly positions in several networking niches, and VMware contracts that are painful to leave.
AVGO.ind: AI networking and custom accelerators growing fast; the legacy semis and software franchises are mature by design.
AVGO.risk: Losing a single custom-silicon customer - the top three are most of AI revenue - or a VMware price backlash driving migration.
AVGO.implied: The price implies custom AI silicon revenue keeps compounding at a very high rate and the VMware price increases stick.
AVGO.debate: Bulls say Broadcom is the only credible alternative to NVIDIA for hyperscaler silicon. Bears note extreme customer concentration and a debt-funded roll-up model.
AVGO.disprove: A named hyperscaler moving its next-generation accelerator elsewhere; VMware renewal churn showing in software growth; free cash flow not covering the acquisition debt schedule.

TSLA.what: Sells electric vehicles, stationary batteries and energy services, and is betting the company on autonomy and robotics.
TSLA.rev: Automotive roughly 75-80% of revenue, energy generation and storage the fastest-growing segment at ~12-15%, services the rest. US, China and Europe are the three markets.
TSLA.gm: Gross margin has fallen from the low 30s to the high teens as prices were cut to defend volume; energy storage now carries a higher margin than cars.
TSLA.mgmt: Elon Musk holds roughly 13% plus a contested compensation award; he divides attention across several companies, which the board treats as acceptable.
TSLA.comp: BYD and Chinese EV makers on price, legacy OEMs (VW, Hyundai, GM) on volume, Waymo on autonomy.
TSLA.moat: Brand, charging network, manufacturing cost leadership outside China and a fleet data advantage - but every element is being competed away.
TSLA.ind: Global EV adoption still growing, but price competition is brutal and US incentives have weakened.
TSLA.risk: Full self-driving failing to reach regulatory approval at scale, leaving the valuation resting on a car business with shrinking margins.
TSLA.implied: The price implies robotaxi and Optimus become real, large, high-margin businesses. On cars alone the multiple is indefensible.
TSLA.debate: Bulls underwrite autonomy and humanoid robots as option value. Bears say deliveries are flat, margins are compressing and the multiple is a belief system.
TSLA.disprove: Unsupervised robotaxi timelines slipping again; automotive gross margin ex-credits below the mid-teens; deliveries declining year over year; regulatory credit revenue disappearing.

MU.what: Sells DRAM and NAND memory - increasingly high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators - to data centre, mobile and auto customers.
MU.rev: DRAM is roughly 75-80% of revenue and nearly all of profit; NAND the rest. Data centre is now the largest end market, driven by HBM.
MU.gm: Gross margin swings from negative to above 50% across the cycle. Memory is a commodity: margin is set by industry supply discipline, not by Micron.
MU.mgmt: Sanjay Mehrotra has been CEO since 2017. Insider ownership is minimal; this is a capital-intensive cyclical run by professional managers.
MU.comp: Samsung and SK Hynix - a three-player oligopoly in DRAM - plus Kioxia and YMTC in NAND.
MU.moat: Scale and process technology in a genuine oligopoly, plus HBM qualification cycles that lock supply a year ahead. The moat is the industry structure, not the company.
MU.ind: Structurally growing with AI memory intensity, but still a capacity cycle that has always mean-reverted.
MU.risk: The classic memory glut: all three players adding capacity into a demand pause, and pricing collapsing within two quarters.
MU.implied: At this price the market is treating HBM as a secular growth business rather than the peak of a cycle. Check the P/E against peak earnings, not trailing.
MU.debate: Bulls say AI memory demand has broken the old cycle and HBM is sold out on contract. Bears note every memory upcycle in forty years ended the same way.
MU.disprove: DRAM spot prices falling for two months; HBM capacity additions from all three suppliers; inventory days rising; customers pushing out qualification.

BRK.B.what: Owns insurance (GEICO, Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance), a railroad, energy utilities, a spread of industrial and retail businesses, and a large listed equity portfolio.
BRK.B.rev: Insurance, BNSF railroad, Berkshire Hathaway Energy and the manufacturing/service/retail group. Float from insurance funds the investments. Almost entirely US.
BRK.B.gm: Not a meaningful metric for a conglomerate; watch operating earnings by segment and the cost of insurance float, which has often been negative.
BRK.B.mgmt: Greg Abel has taken over as CEO with Warren Buffett as chairman; Buffett still holds a large economic stake. Insider alignment is exceptional.
BRK.B.comp: Other insurers (Progressive, Chubb) and other acquirers of private businesses (Brookfield, private equity) competing for deals.
BRK.B.moat: Permanent capital, a cost-of-float advantage, and a reputation that makes Berkshire the buyer of choice in a crisis. Size is now the constraint.
BRK.B.ind: Mature businesses; the interesting variable is what gets done with the cash pile.
BRK.B.risk: Succession without Buffett changing the culture or the deal flow - or a mega-catastrophe insurance year colliding with an equity drawdown.
BRK.B.implied: It trades on book value, not earnings. The price implies modest premium to book with cash earning short-term rates.
BRK.B.debate: Bulls say a fortress balance sheet with a vast cash pile is an option on market dislocation. Bears say the size makes double-digit compounding arithmetically hard.
BRK.B.disprove: Price to book stretching above historical range; underwriting losses at GEICO; large acquisitions at prices the old Berkshire would not have paid.

LLY.what: Sells prescription drugs - above all the GLP-1 incretins tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) - to patients through payers and health systems.
LLY.rev: Incretins are over half of revenue and nearly all of the growth; oncology (Verzenio), immunology, neuroscience (Kisunla) the rest. US roughly 70%.
LLY.gm: Gross margin around 80-83%. Patented biologics with enormous pricing power in the US, though manufacturing scale-up and net price rebates weigh on it.
LLY.mgmt: David Ricks is CEO. Insider ownership is low, but the Lilly Endowment holds a large block, which gives long-horizon stability.
LLY.comp: Novo Nordisk head-on in incretins, with Amgen, Pfizer, Viking and Chinese biotechs pursuing oral and next-generation obesity drugs.
LLY.moat: Patents to the mid-2030s, manufacturing capacity that took years and billions to build, and clinical data breadth across obesity, diabetes, sleep apnoea and heart failure.
LLY.ind: The obesity market is the fastest-growing drug category in history and is still supply-constrained.
LLY.risk: US drug-pricing action on GLP-1s, or an oral competitor with comparable efficacy and far lower cost of goods.
LLY.implied: A P/E in the 30s on rapidly growing earnings implies incretin revenue roughly doubling again with pricing holding up.
LLY.debate: Bulls model a $150bn+ obesity market with two credible suppliers. Bears point at Medicare pricing negotiation, compounders and orals arriving in force.
LLY.disprove: US net price per script falling faster than volume growth; a competitor oral matching 20%+ weight loss with clean safety; scripts plateauing; capacity expansion outrunning demand.

JPM.what: The largest US bank: lends to and banks consumers, corporates and institutions, and runs a top-three investment bank and asset manager.
JPM.rev: Consumer and community banking ~35-40%, corporate and investment bank ~35%, asset and wealth management ~15%, commercial banking the rest. Mostly US.
JPM.gm: Banks do not report gross margin. Watch net interest margin, efficiency ratio (around 50-55%) and return on tangible equity, which has run near 20%.
JPM.mgmt: Jamie Dimon has run it since 2005 and holds a substantial personal stake; succession is the open governance question.
JPM.comp: Bank of America, Citigroup and Wells Fargo domestically; Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley in markets and advisory.
JPM.moat: Scale in deposits and technology spend, regulatory capital requirements that deter entry, and a genuine fortress balance sheet that wins share in every crisis.
JPM.ind: Mature and cyclical; deposit share keeps concentrating in the largest banks.
JPM.risk: A credit cycle - commercial real estate or consumer - arriving while rates fall and net interest income compresses.
JPM.implied: Around two times tangible book implies sustained high-teens returns on tangible equity, well above the sector.
JPM.debate: Bulls say it is the best-run bank in the world and deserves a premium. Bears say you are buying a cyclical at peak earnings and peak book multiple.
JPM.disprove: Net charge-offs rising faster than guidance; reserve builds accelerating; net interest income guidance cut; ROTCE falling below the mid-teens.

WMT.what: Sells groceries and general merchandise to about 250 million weekly customers, increasingly online and increasingly with advertising attached.
WMT.rev: Walmart US ~68%, Walmart International ~18%, Sams Club ~14%. Grocery is roughly 60% of US sales - it is a grocer with a media business attached.
WMT.gm: Gross margin around 24-25%. Retail scale means buying power, but grocery is structurally low margin; the profit growth is coming from advertising and membership.
WMT.mgmt: John Furner is CEO, succeeding Doug McMillon after a long tenure; the Walton family still owns roughly 45% of the shares.
WMT.comp: Amazon, Costco, Target and Kroger, plus dollar stores at the value end.
WMT.moat: Purchasing scale, a store network within ten miles of most Americans doubling as fulfilment nodes, and an everyday-low-price reputation.
WMT.ind: Grocery grows with population and inflation; the share shift online and into retail media is the real story.
WMT.risk: A price war with Amazon on grocery delivery, or consumer trade-down that arrives without the offsetting mix benefit.
WMT.implied: A P/E in the 30s for a retailer growing sales mid single digits implies advertising and membership keep expanding the margin every year.
WMT.debate: Bulls say the high-margin ad and marketplace layer re-rates the whole company. Bears say it is still a grocer priced like a software company.
WMT.disprove: US comparable sales slowing below 3%; e-commerce losses widening; advertising growth decelerating; operating margin failing to expand.

AMD.what: Sells CPUs and GPUs for data centres, PCs and gaming consoles - the credible second source to Intel and NVIDIA.
AMD.rev: Data centre is roughly half of revenue (EPYC server CPUs plus Instinct accelerators), client PCs about a third, gaming and embedded the rest.
AMD.gm: Gross margin around 50-54%. Fabless with TSMC; server CPUs carry high margin, AI accelerators currently lower than NVIDIA equivalents.
AMD.mgmt: Lisa Su has run the turnaround since 2014 and is widely regarded as one of the best operators in the industry; insider ownership is small.
AMD.comp: Intel in x86 server and client CPUs, NVIDIA in AI accelerators, Arm-based designs from Amazon and Ampere.
AMD.moat: Process-node leadership through TSMC and a chiplet architecture that is genuinely ahead of Intel - but no CUDA equivalent on the GPU side.
AMD.ind: Server CPU share shifting to AMD; the AI accelerator market is growing but NVIDIA holds it.
AMD.risk: ROCm failing to reach parity with CUDA, so AI revenue stays a rounding error against expectations - or Intel recovering on 18A.
AMD.implied: The valuation implies AMD takes a meaningful double-digit share of AI accelerator spend within a few years.
AMD.debate: Bulls say any second source in a supply-constrained market wins billions. Bears say software is the barrier and AMD has not cleared it.
AMD.disprove: Instinct revenue guidance missed twice; hyperscalers naming custom silicon over AMD; server CPU share gains stalling; gross margin sliding as accelerator mix rises.

V.what: Runs the rails for card payments between banks, merchants and consumers - it does not lend, it takes a toll on volume.
V.rev: Service, data processing, international transaction and other revenues, net of client incentives. Cross-border volume carries far higher take rates. US roughly 40% of revenue.
V.gm: Operating margin runs near 65-67%, among the highest of any large company. The network is built; each additional transaction costs almost nothing.
V.mgmt: Ryan McInerney is CEO. Insider ownership is negligible; capital returns are steady and large.
V.comp: Mastercard as the near-twin, American Express in premium, plus account-to-account rails (Pix, UPI, FedNow) and stablecoins as the structural threat.
V.moat: Two-sided network effects across 150 million merchants and 4 billion cards, plus decades of settlement, fraud and regulatory infrastructure.
V.ind: Cash-to-card conversion continues globally; developed-market volume growth is now mostly nominal GDP plus a little.
V.risk: Regulated real-time account-to-account rails in major markets bypassing the card networks - the Pix outcome repeated elsewhere.
V.implied: A high-20s P/E implies low-double-digit revenue growth indefinitely with no take-rate compression.
V.debate: Bulls call it a toll on global consumption with software margins. Bears watch governments building public payment rails that do the same job for free.
V.disprove: Take rate declining; cross-border volume growth slowing sharply; a major market mandating A2A acceptance; client incentives growing faster than gross revenue.

XOM.what: Finds, produces, refines and sells oil, gas and chemicals worldwide.
XOM.rev: Upstream production (Permian and Guyana are the crown jewels), energy products (refining), chemical products and specialty products. Global, with US the largest single market.
XOM.gm: Not the right metric. Watch upstream unit costs, refining crack spreads and the cash break-even oil price - Exxon has pushed break-even into the $30s per barrel.
XOM.mgmt: Darren Woods is CEO. Insider ownership is small; capital discipline and a rising dividend are the stated policy.
XOM.comp: Chevron, Shell, BP, TotalEnergies and the national oil companies.
XOM.moat: Low-cost resource position in Guyana and the Permian, integration across the barrel, and a scale of project execution few can match.
XOM.ind: Oil demand is still growing modestly but is a declining share of energy; refining capacity is tight.
XOM.risk: A sustained oil price below the mid $50s, which would squeeze the dividend-plus-buyback commitment.
XOM.implied: The multiple implies mid-cycle oil prices holding and Guyana volumes ramping as planned.
XOM.debate: Bulls point to the lowest-cost barrels in the industry and decades of reserve life. Bears say terminal demand risk caps the multiple permanently.
XOM.disprove: Guyana production or cost guidance slipping; break-even creeping up; buybacks funded by debt; reserve replacement below 100%.

JNJ.what: Sells prescription medicines (immunology, oncology, neuroscience) and medical devices (surgery, orthopaedics, vision) to health systems.
JNJ.rev: Innovative Medicine roughly 65%, MedTech roughly 35% after the consumer spin-off of Kenvue. US just over half of revenue.
JNJ.gm: Gross margin around 68-70%. Patented drugs are high margin; devices are lower and more manufacturing-intensive.
JNJ.mgmt: Joaquin Duato is CEO. Insider ownership is minimal; the dividend has been raised for more than sixty consecutive years.
JNJ.comp: AbbVie, Merck and Pfizer in pharma; Medtronic, Stryker and Abbott in devices.
JNJ.moat: Patent portfolio, surgeon training and hospital relationships in devices, and a balance sheet rated higher than most governments.
JNJ.ind: Mature and defensive; growth comes from the pipeline and from an ageing population.
JNJ.risk: The talc litigation resolving badly, or the Stelara biosimilar erosion running faster than the new launches can offset.
JNJ.implied: A high-teens P/E implies mid single-digit growth with litigation contained - a modest bar.
JNJ.debate: Bulls like the defensiveness and the pipeline depth at a reasonable multiple. Bears see a patent cliff and an unresolved legal overhang.
JNJ.disprove: Stelara erosion faster than guided; talc settlement above reserves; MedTech growth below market; pipeline readouts failing.

INTC.what: Designs and manufactures x86 CPUs, and is trying to become a contract foundry for other chip designers.
INTC.rev: Client computing (PC CPUs) roughly half, data centre and AI about a third, foundry services and other the rest.
INTC.gm: Gross margin has fallen from 60%+ to the 30s-40s. Owning fabs means enormous fixed costs; under-utilisation destroys the margin.
INTC.mgmt: Lip-Bu Tan took over in 2025 with a mandate to cut costs and fix the foundry. The US government took an equity stake as part of CHIPS support.
INTC.comp: AMD in x86, TSMC in foundry, NVIDIA in accelerators, Arm-based designs across the board.
INTC.moat: What is left of it is scale in x86 and government-backed domestic manufacturing. The technology lead is gone - treat the moat as impaired.
INTC.ind: PCs are flat, data centre CPUs are losing share to AMD and accelerators; foundry is growing but dominated by TSMC.
INTC.risk: 18A or 14A failing to win a major external foundry customer, leaving a capital-intensive business with no path to scale.
INTC.implied: The price now embeds a foundry turnaround. On current earnings power the multiple is not supportable.
INTC.debate: Bulls see a national-champion turnaround with government support and a cheap asset base. Bears see two decades of execution failure and negative free cash flow.
INTC.disprove: No named external 18A/14A customer with volume; capex not funded from operations; further share loss in server CPUs; foundry losses widening.

MA.what: Runs a global card payment network, connecting issuers and merchants for a fee on volume.
MA.rev: Payment network fees plus a fast-growing value-added services and solutions arm (fraud, data, consulting) that is now roughly a third of revenue.
MA.gm: Operating margin around 55-58%. Same network economics as Visa: fixed infrastructure, near-zero marginal cost.
MA.mgmt: Michael Miebach is CEO. The Mastercard Foundation holds a large block, giving a long-term anchor shareholder.
MA.comp: Visa above all, American Express in premium, domestic schemes and real-time payment rails everywhere.
MA.moat: Network effects, regulatory complexity and a services layer that increases merchant and issuer switching costs.
MA.ind: Same as Visa: cash conversion plus cross-border travel recovery, with A2A rails as the long-term threat.
MA.implied: A high-30s P/E implies sustained mid-teens earnings growth - a demanding bar even for this quality.
MA.risk: Regulated domestic rails displacing card acceptance in large markets, or interchange regulation in the US.
MA.debate: Bulls say value-added services justify the premium to Visa. Bears note it is the more expensive of two near-identical businesses.
MA.disprove: Cross-border volume growth normalising to low single digits; services growth slowing; regulatory caps on interchange in the US; take rate falling.

ABBV.what: Sells immunology drugs (Skyrizi, Rinvoq), aesthetics (Botox) and neuroscience treatments, after losing Humira exclusivity.
ABBV.rev: Immunology is roughly half of revenue, with Skyrizi and Rinvoq now well past Humira; aesthetics, neuroscience and oncology the rest. US around 75%.
ABBV.gm: Gross margin around 70% on a reported basis, higher adjusted. Patented biologics with US pricing power; aesthetics is a cash-pay consumer business.
ABBV.mgmt: Robert Michael is CEO following Richard Gonzalez. Insider ownership is small; the dividend is the stated priority.
ABBV.comp: J&J and Pfizer in immunology, Merck and BMS in oncology, plus biosimilar manufacturers.
ABBV.moat: Formulary position, patent estates on the new immunology pair, and the Botox brand in a cash-pay market.
ABBV.ind: Immunology is growing; aesthetics is cyclical and has been weak.
ABBV.risk: Skyrizi and Rinvoq facing Medicare price negotiation late this decade before the next wave of launches arrives.
ABBV.implied: The multiple implies the immunology pair keeps compounding to $30bn+ combined with no pricing shock.
ABBV.debate: Bulls say ABBV navigated the largest patent cliff in history and now has two mega-brands. Bears point to a heavy debt load and the next cliff already visible.
ABBV.disprove: Skyrizi or Rinvoq script growth decelerating; aesthetics declining further; net debt not falling; IRA negotiation including the immunology pair.
